items.title: Linear equations and systems
items.when: Undo operations in reverse order. Substitute or eliminate a variable in a system; verify both original equations. A zero coefficient can produce no solution or infinitely many.
items.example: For 3x−4=11, x=5. In x+y=9 and 2x−y=6, adding gives x=5 and then y=4.

items.title: Quadratic formula and discriminant
items.when: First set ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. D>0 gives two real roots, D=0 one repeated real root, and D<0 two nonreal complex roots.
items.example: For x²−4x−1=0, D=20 and \(x=2\pm\sqrt5\). Substituting either root gives zero.

items.title: Vertex and completing the square
items.when: For a≠0, the vertex is (h,k). Positive a means a minimum; negative a a maximum. For a restricted interval, also test allowed endpoints.

items.title: Factoring and root relationships
items.when: Factor out the greatest common factor first. The sum/product formulas apply to a quadratic with a≠0, including complex roots. Never cancel terms across addition.
items.example: \(3x^2-12=3(x-2)(x+2)\). Roots of 4x²−12x+5 sum to 3 and multiply to 5/4.

items.title: Sum and difference of cubes
items.when: The second factor has the opposite middle sign. Check a factorization by multiplying; a sum of squares does not factor over the reals in the same way.

items.title: Remainder and factor theorems
items.when: When dividing by x−r, the remainder is P(r). The divisor is a factor exactly when P(r)=0. For x+r, substitute −r.
items.example: For P(x)=x³−2x+1, dividing by x−3 leaves P(3)=27−6+1=22.

items.title: Absolute value equations and inequalities
items.when: The displayed inequality rules assume a>0. Use inclusive endpoints for ≤ or ≥. An absolute value cannot equal a negative number.

items.title: Rational equations and sign charts
items.when: Exclude every original zero denominator before canceling. For inequalities, mark zeros of both numerator and denominator, then test each interval. A denominator zero is always excluded.
items.example: \(\frac{x-1}{x+4}>0\) is true for x<−4 or x>1; both boundary points are excluded.

items.title: Radical equations and extraneous roots
items.when: Squaring can create false solutions. Check each candidate in the original equation, including its sign restrictions.
items.example: \(\sqrt{x+6}=x\) gives x²−x−6=0. Only x=3 works; candidate −2 is negative.

items.title: Linear and quadratic inequalities
items.when: Reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative. For a quadratic product, use its real zeros to split the number line and test signs.
items.example: −3x≥12 means x≤−4. Also (x−2)(x+5)<0 means −5<x<2.

items.title: Evaluation and composition
items.when: Evaluate the inner function first. In a piecewise function, choose the branch using its input before calculating. Composition is different from multiplication.
items.example: If f(x)=x²+2 and g(x)=2x−3, then f(g(4))=f(5)=27.

items.title: Domain and range
items.when: Intersect every restriction, including inner and outer functions in a composition. A canceled factor still excludes its original input. Range concerns outputs, not inputs.
items.example: \(\frac{\sqrt{7-x}}{x+2}\) permits x≤7 except x=−2.

items.title: Graph transformations
items.when: With a,b≠0, a feature at (u,v) moves to (h+u/b,k+av). Negative a reflects outputs; negative b reflects inputs. Apply horizontal changes inside the function.
items.example: If f has a point (6,2), then g(x)=3f(2(x−1))−4 has the corresponding point (4,2).

items.title: Inverse functions and branches
items.when: Solve for the original input and respect its domain. An inverse function requires one-to-one behavior, often enforced by restricting a quadratic to one side of its vertex.

items.title: Slope and average rate of change
items.when: Inputs must differ. Keep the same subtraction order in numerator and denominator. Average rate is the slope of the secant, even when the function is curved.
items.example: For f(x)=x²+1 from x=1 to x=4, average rate=(17−2)/(4−1)=5.

items.title: Even and odd symmetry
items.when: The domain must allow both x and −x. For polynomials, all nonconstant terms in an even function have even powers; an odd polynomial has only odd powers and no nonzero constant.
items.example: x⁴−3x²+2 is even; 2x³−x is odd; x²+x is neither.

items.title: Zeros, holes, and asymptotes
items.when: Cancel common factors first, retaining restrictions. A finite missing value is a hole; a remaining denominator zero typically gives a vertical asymptote. Leading terms describe end behavior.
items.example: \(\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}\) has a hole at (2,4). For 1/(x−5), the vertical asymptote is x=5.

items.title: Direct and inverse variation
items.when: For direct variation, y/x is constant when x≠0. For inverse variation, xy is constant and x cannot be zero. A nonzero intercept breaks direct proportionality.
items.example: If y varies inversely with x and y=8 when x=3, k=24 and y=4 when x=6.

items.title: Exponential growth and decay
items.when: For real-time models use b>0; a is the value at t=0. Equal time gaps have equal ratios. Repeated p% growth uses b=1+p/100; decay uses b=1−p/100.
items.example: A quantity growing from 18 at t=1 to 144 at t=4 has b³=8, b=2, and a=9.

items.title: Logarithms and their rules
items.when: For real logarithms b>0, b≠1, and original arguments must be positive. Use u,v>0 for these rules. Change of base is log_b(u)=ln(u)/ln(b). No logarithm rule splits a sum.
items.example: \(\log_2(x+3)-\log_2(x-1)=1\) requires x>1 and gives (x+3)/(x−1)=2, so x=5.

title: Geometry: coordinates, shapes, and spatial reasoning

items.title: Plane areas and perimeters
items.when: Heights are perpendicular to their bases. Perimeter adds exposed boundary lengths. Composite areas add included pieces and subtract cutouts; convert all lengths first.
items.example: A trapezoid with parallel sides 6 and 12 and perpendicular height 5 has area (6+12)5/2=45.

items.title: Triangle lengths and angles
items.when: Pythagoras requires a right triangle and c opposite 90°. In every nondegenerate triangle, each side is strictly between the difference and sum of the others.
items.example: A right triangle with legs 9 and 12 has hypotenuse 15. Sides 5 and 11 require 6<c<16.

items.title: Special triangles and equilateral area
items.when: Associate each side with its opposite angle. The hypotenuse is always largest; the longer leg in a 30° triangle is not half the hypotenuse.
items.example: An equilateral triangle with side 6 has altitude 3√3 and area 9√3.

items.title: Heron and the angle bisector
items.when: Heron uses three sides of a valid triangle. The ratio applies when AD bisects angle A and D lies on BC. Split the whole opposite side according to that ratio.
items.example: Sides 5,5,6 give s=8 and area √(8·3·3·2)=12. A bisector between sides 4 and 6 splits an opposite side of 15 into 6 and 9.

items.title: Polygon and parallel-line angles
items.when: Regular means all sides and angles are equal. Corresponding and alternate interior angles agree for parallel lines; adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
items.example: A regular nonagon has interior angle 140° and exterior angle 40°.

items.title: Similarity and scale
items.when: Match corresponding dimensions first. Area and volume ratios only follow from similarity of the entire figures. Take a square or cube root to recover a length factor.
items.example: Similar solids with volume ratio 27:64 have length ratio 3:4 and surface-area ratio 9:16.

items.title: Circle, ring, arc, and sector
items.when: The last two formulas require θ in radians. For degrees multiply circumference or area by θ/360. Radius is half the diameter; arc length has linear units.
items.example: A radius-5 sector of angle 72° has arc length 2π and area 5π; the equivalent radian angle is \(2\pi/5\).

items.title: Circle angles and intersecting segments
items.formula: \(\text{inscribed angle}=\tfrac12\text{intercepted arc};\quad AP\cdot PB=CP\cdot PD;\quad t^2=e(e+i)\)
items.when: The chord-product relation uses two chords crossing at interior P. The tangent-secant relation uses outside length e and inside length i from one exterior point. A tangent is perpendicular to its radius.
items.example: Chord parts 3,8 and 4,x give x=6. A secant with outside part 4 and inside part 5 gives tangent length 6.

items.title: Lines, distance, and midpoint
items.when: Slope is Δy/Δx for nonvertical lines. Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular nonvertical slopes multiply to −1; horizontal and vertical lines are the special pair.
items.example: The line through (2,−1) with slope 3 is y+1=3(x−2). The midpoint of (−2,4) and (6,0) is (2,2).

items.title: Coordinate circles
items.when: Read center (h,k) with reversed signs inside parentheses. In a general circle equation, complete the square in both variables. The right side is radius squared, not radius.
items.example: x²+y²+4x−10y+20=0 becomes (x+2)²+(y−5)²=9, with center (−2,5), radius 3.

items.title: Coordinate transformations
items.when: These rotations are about the origin. For center (h,k), subtract it, rotate, then add it back. Reflection in x-axis: (x,−y); y-axis: (−x,y); y=x: (y,x). Reflect across x=h using x′=2h−x.
items.example: Rotating (3,−2) 90° counterclockwise about the origin gives (2,3). Reflecting (7,1) across x=2 gives (−3,1).

items.title: Prisms, boxes, and cylinders
items.formula: \(V=Bh;\quad V_{\rm box}=lwh;\quad SA_{\rm box}=2(lw+lh+wh);\quad SA_{\rm cylinder}=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\)
items.when: B is base area and h perpendicular height. A right prism has lateral area base perimeter × height. Surface-area formulas assume closed solids; omit absent or hidden faces.
items.example: A closed radius-4 cylinder of height 3 has volume 48π and surface area 56π. A 2×3×4 box has volume 24 and surface area 52.

items.title: Cones, pyramids, and spheres
items.formula: \(V_{\rm cone/pyramid}=Bh/3;\quad SA_{\rm cone}=\pi r^2+\pi r\ell;\quad V_{\rm sphere}=4\pi r^3/3;\quad SA_{\rm sphere}=4\pi r^2\)
items.when: For a right cone, slant height ℓ=√(r²+h²), not vertical height. A regular pyramid has lateral area perimeter × slant height /2. A closed hemisphere also includes its circular base.
items.example: A right cone with radius 3 and height 4 has slant height 5, volume 12π, and total surface area 24π.

items.title: Coordinate area and perpendicular distance
items.when: For a triangle using two adjacent vectors, halve the determinant area. The distance formula assumes Ax+By+C=0 and A,B not both zero. A box diagonal is √(l²+w²+h²).
items.example: Vectors (3,1) and (−2,4) span a triangle of area |12+2|/2=7. Distance from (1,2) to 3x+4y−1=0 is 10/5=2.

title: Trigonometry: exact values and all valid solutions

items.title: Right-triangle ratios
items.when: Use an acute marked angle in a right triangle. Opposite and adjacent depend on that angle. Hypotenuse is opposite 90° and does not change.
items.example: With opposite 7, adjacent 24, hypotenuse 25, sine is 7/25 and tangent 7/24.

items.title: Exact unit-circle values
items.when: Unit-circle points are (cosθ,sinθ). Use a reference angle and the quadrant sign beyond the first quadrant. Tangent is sine/cosine and is undefined when cosine is zero.
items.example: \(\cos(5\pi/6)=-\sqrt3/2\) because the reference angle is π/6 in Quadrant II.

items.title: Radians, arc length, and signs
items.when: Arc length requires radians. Sine is positive in I/II, cosine in I/IV, tangent in I/III. A negative angle is clockwise; its trig values do not all become negative.
items.example: 150°=5π/6 radians. On radius 12 its arc length is 10π.

items.title: Reciprocals and basic identities
items.when: Keep denominator restrictions. A squared sine means (sinθ)². Use quadrant signs when taking a square root to recover sine or cosine.
items.example: If cosθ=−12/13 in Quadrant II, sinθ=5/13, tanθ=−5/12, and secθ=−13/12.

items.title: Double-angle and sum identities
items.formula: \(\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta;\;\cos2\theta=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta;\;\sin(u\pm v)=\sin u\cos v\pm\cos u\sin v;\;\cos(u\pm v)=\cos u\cos v\mp\sin u\sin v\)
items.when: Use the opposite sign in the cosine sum rule. Double-angle forms include 2cos²θ−1 and 1−2sin²θ. These formulas do not remove any restriction from an original denominator.
items.example: \(\sin75^\circ=\sin(45^\circ+30^\circ)=(\sqrt6+\sqrt2)/4\).

items.title: Trig graphs and intervals
items.when: For nonconstant sine/cosine, A,B≠0. Tangent has period π/|B| and no finite amplitude. Restricted intervals can shrink the sine/cosine range. Inverse trig gives one angle, so count all solutions.
items.example: For 4cos(2x−π)+1, amplitude=4, period=π, shift=π/2 right, and full-domain range=[−3,5].

items.title: Laws of sines and cosines
items.formula: \(a/\sin A=b/\sin B=c/\sin C;\quad c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C;\quad K=ab\sin C/2\)
items.when: Lowercase side a is opposite angle A. Cosine law uses the included angle. A nonincluded angle with two sides can produce zero, one, or two triangles; test the supplement and the 180° sum.
items.example: Sides 6 and 10 enclosing 60° give third side √76=2√19 and area 15√3.

items.title: Elevation and angle solutions
items.when: The height formula uses horizontal distance d and elevation θ from horizontal; add observer eye height if needed. For a trig equation, solve for its entire inner angle, then restrict x to the stated interval.
items.example: At horizontal distance 18 and elevation 45°, the rise is 18. With eye height 1.5, total height is 19.5.

items.title: Mean, weighted mean, median, and mode
items.formula: \(\bar x=\frac{\sum x_i}{n};\quad\bar x_{\rm weighted}=\frac{\sum n_i\bar x_i}{\sum n_i}\)
items.when: Use counts as weights, including in frequency tables. Sort before locating a median; an even count uses the average of two middle entries. Mode is the most frequent value.
items.example: Four values averaging 7 and six averaging 12 combine to mean (28+72)/10=10.

items.title: Spread, variance, and standardized distance
items.when: Population variance divides by N; sample variance by n−1 with n>1. Standard deviation is the square root. z requires σ>0 and does not by itself establish a normal distribution.
items.example: The population 1,3,5 has mean 3, variance 8/3, and standard deviation √(8/3).

items.title: Transforming every data value
items.when: Adding a constant does not change spread. A negative multiplier reverses order but standard deviation stays nonnegative. Do not multiply variance by |a|.
items.example: If mean=20 and standard deviation=4, y=−3x+10 has mean −50, standard deviation 12, variance 144.

items.title: Conditional and joint probability
items.when: Conditioning requires P(B)>0 and changes the denominator to the given group. Without replacement, counts change after each draw. Independence means P(A|B)=P(A) when conditioning is defined.
items.example: If 9 of 15 cyclists wear helmets, among cyclists the helmet probability is 9/15=3/5, regardless of the number of noncyclists.

items.title: Union and complements
items.when: Disjoint events have no overlap. Independent events may overlap; then multiply to get the overlap. “At least one” is often 1 minus the probability of none.
items.example: With P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.3, and overlap=0.1, the inclusive union is 0.8.

items.title: Permutations, combinations, and repeated objects
items.when: Use permutations for ordered choices without repeats, combinations for unordered choices. For arrangements with indistinguishable repeats, divide by each repeat count factorial. All counts are nonnegative integers and r≤n.
items.example: Three roles from six people give 120 assignments; three-person groups give 20. BANANA has 6!/(3!2!)=60 distinct arrangements.

items.title: Binomial probability and expected value
items.when: Binomial trials must be independent with a fixed count n and unchanged success probability p. Distribution probabilities sum to 1. Subtract entry costs for net gains.
items.example: In four independent fair trials, exactly one success has probability 4/16=1/4. A $9 payout with chance 1/3 and $2 entry cost has expected net gain $1.

items.title: Randomization, association, and residuals
items.when: Random sampling supports population generalization; random treatment assignment supports causal comparison under a sound design. Association alone does not establish cause. Systematic residual patterns suggest a model misses structure.
items.example: A model predicts 18 when the observed value is 15, so residual=−3. This indicates overprediction, not an error of +3.

title: Number and quantity: structure, vectors, and matrices

items.title: Exponent rules and scientific notation
items.when: Use nonzero bases for zero/negative exponents and denominators. These identities hold for integer exponents; with arbitrary real exponents take a>0. Normalize scientific notation as c·10ⁿ with 1≤|c|<10.
items.example: \(\frac{6\times10^7}{3\times10^{-2}}=2\times10^9\). A negative denominator exponent is subtracted.

items.title: Radicals and rational exponents
items.when: Reduce the rational exponent first and state the real domain. Even roots need nonnegative radicands; negative powers also exclude zero. Do not distribute a radical across a sum.

items.title: Complex numbers, conjugates, and magnitude
items.when: Powers of i cycle every four. Rationalize a complex denominator by its conjugate, assuming the denominator is nonzero. A squared complex number and squared magnitude differ.

items.title: Vector operations and dot product
items.formula: \(\mathbf u+\mathbf v=(u_x+v_x,u_y+v_y);\quad|\mathbf u|=\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2};\quad\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=u_xv_x+u_yv_y=|\mathbf u||\mathbf v|\cos\theta\)
items.when: Scalar multiplication applies to every component. Dot product zero implies perpendicularity only for two nonzero vectors. The angle formula divides by both magnitudes.
items.example: For u=(1,−2), v=(4,2), the dot product is 0, so they are perpendicular. The vector 3u−v is (−1,−8).

items.title: Matrix addition, scalar multiplication, and products
items.when: Add/subtract matrices only if their dimensions match; scalar multiplication changes every entry. Multiplication needs matching inner dimensions and uses row-column dot products. Usually AB≠BA.
items.example: \(\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\\2\end{bmatrix}\).

items.title: Determinant and 2×2 inverse
items.when: An inverse exists only if ad−bc≠0. Verify by multiplying to the identity. Swap the diagonal entries and negate the off-diagonal entries before dividing by the determinant.
items.example: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\) has determinant 1 and inverse \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}\).

items.title: Arithmetic terms and sums
items.when: An arithmetic sequence has constant differences. The formula starts at index 1; with index 0 use a_n=a_0+nd. Distinguish the nth term from the sum of n terms.
items.example: For first term 4, difference 5, the tenth term is 49 and first-ten sum is 10(4+49)/2=265.

items.title: Geometric terms and finite/infinite sums
items.when: The finite sum formula assumes r≠1; if r=1, S_n=na_1. The infinite sum exists only when |r|<1. Count n−1 jumps from the first to nth term.
items.example: For 20,10,5,…, the fifth term is 5/4, the first-five sum is 155/4, and the infinite sum is 40.

items.title: Prime factors, GCF, LCM, and remainders
items.when: For the GCF/LCM identity use positive integers. Prime factors with smaller exponents give the GCF; larger exponents give the LCM. An even plus an odd integer is odd; the product is even.
items.example: 60=2²·3·5 and 84=2²·3·7 have GCF 12 and LCM 420. Since N=7q+4, 2N+1 leaves remainder 2 on division by 7.

title: Essential skills: proportions, rates, and quantities

items.title: Percent change and reversing changes
items.when: Percent change needs a nonzero original base. Successive changes multiply factors. Reverse by dividing by the factor; a p% rise and p% fall do not cancel.
items.example: After a 30% discount a price is $84, so the original price was 84/0.70=$120.

items.title: Ratios and proportions
items.when: Use a,b≥0 with positive sum. Cross-multiply a/b=c/d only when denominators are nonzero. Compare like units before forming a ratio.
items.example: A 2:7 split of 81 gives 18 and 63; the smaller portion is 2/9 of the whole.

items.title: Rate, distance, density, and units
items.when: Use compatible units and positive elapsed time. Average speeds directly only with equal times. A squared or cubed unit conversion uses the conversion factor twice or three times.
items.example: Traveling 36 miles at 18 mph then 24 at 24 mph takes 3 hours total, giving an average of 20 mph.

items.title: Work rates and relative motion
items.when: Solo times are positive. Add filling rates and subtract draining rates. Add speeds toward each other; subtract for a same-direction chase. A zero or negative net filling rate cannot fill an empty tank.
items.example: Machines needing 6 and 9 hours alone work at rate 5/18, so together need 18/5 hours.

items.title: Mixtures and weighted quantities
items.when: Use compatible volume units and decimal concentrations. Pure water has concentration 0, pure ingredient 1. The final concentration lies between the input concentrations.
items.example: Combining 3 liters at 20% and 7 at 40% gives (0.6+2.8)/10=34%.

items.title: Estimation and whole-number rounding
items.when: Round only at the end unless the question specifies otherwise. For positive quantities, round up capacity needs and down budget limits. Use units and an estimate to catch misplaced decimals.
items.example: For 97 guests at tables of 8, 12 tables are insufficient, so ceil(97/8)=13 tables are needed.

items.title: Linear models and break-even
items.when: F is fixed cost, v cost per unit, and p selling price. Break-even requires R=C. Check domain and whole-unit constraints; if p≤v and F>0, positive production cannot cover the fixed cost.
items.example: With fixed cost 120, cost 3 per item and price 8, break-even is q=120/(8−3)=24.

items.title: Simple and compound interest
items.when: r is annual rate as a decimal, t years, and n compounding periods per year. These models exclude additional deposits/withdrawals. Do not use a percent as a whole number.
items.example: With $500 at 6% compounded twice yearly for 3 years, amount is 500(1.03)⁶; simple interest would give $590.

items.title: Doubling time and half-life
items.when: Use consistent time units. d is doubling time and h half-life. These assume a constant exponential rate; they do not describe constant absolute gains or losses.
items.example: An 80-unit sample with half-life 6 hours has 80(1/2)³=10 units after 18 hours.

items.title: Quadratic optimization with constraints
items.when: For a<0 the unrestricted vertex maximizes output. Compare it with allowed interval endpoints. For whole counts, check nearby feasible integers; the vertex input is different from its output.
items.example: For P(q)=−q²+14q−10 on 0≤q≤5, the unrestricted vertex q=7 is unavailable; maximum P(5)=35.

items.title: Thresholds and piecewise costs
items.when: This model has F covering the first q₀ units and rate r on excess units. State whether thresholds include equality and whether a charge rounds up fractional units.
items.example: A $12 plan includes 4 visits, then charges $3 per extra visit. Nine visits cost 12+3(9−4)=$27.

items.title: Recovering and judging models
items.when: Use differences for a stated linear model and ratios across equal gaps for an exponential one. Small residuals suggest fit only on the observed data; systematic residual patterns signal missing structure.
items.example: A linear model has outputs 17 at x=2 and 29 at x=5, giving m=4 and b=9. At x=3, observed 20 minus predicted 21 gives residual −1.
